summary_en: A family outing to the Acropolis: prepositions with the genitive, dative and accusative, and verbs built with a preposition in front.

grammar.md:
**Prepositions and their cases.** You already use ἐν + dative, εἰς + accusative and ἐκ + genitive. The pattern behind them runs through the whole language: **genitive** for *away from*, **dative** for *at rest, position*, **accusative** for *motion towards*.

| | + genitive | + dative | + accusative |
|---|---|---|---|
| ἐν | | in | |
| εἰς | | | into, to |
| ἐκ / ἐξ | out of | | |
| **ἀπό** | away from: ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς | | |
| **πρός** | | | towards, to: πρὸς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν |
| **μετά** | with: μετὰ τῶν παίδων | | (after — Unit 6) |
| **ἐπί** | on: ἐπὶ τῆς ἀκροπόλεως | at, by: ἐπὶ τῇ θύρᾳ | onto, up to: ἐπὶ τὸ τεῖχος |
| ὑπό | | under: ὑπὸ τῷ δένδρῳ | |

ἐπί is the best example: one preposition, three cases, three shades of meaning. ἐκ becomes ἐξ before a vowel (ἐξ ἀγορᾶς), and ἀπό, μετά, ἐπί, ὑπό drop their final vowel before one (ἀπ' οἴκου, μετ' αὐτοῦ). Prepositions never take an accent-shift onto the article: ἀπὸ τῆς, πρὸς τήν.

**Compound verbs.** A preposition can be glued to the front of a verb: ἀνα-βαίνω *go up*, κατα-βαίνω *go down*, εἰσ-έρχομαι *go in*, ἐξ-έρχομαι *go out* (ἐκ → ἐξ before the vowel), προσ-έρχομαι *approach*. The verb part conjugates exactly as before: ἀναβαίνει, ἀναβαίνουσιν; εἰσέρχεται, εἰσέρχονται. Greek likes to repeat the preposition after the verb: **εἰς** τὴν ἀκρόπολιν **εἰσ**έρχονται, **ἐκ** τῆς οἰκίας **ἐξ**έρχεται, **πρὸς** τὸ ἄγαλμα **προσ**έρχεται.

**Neuter plural, singular verb.** τὰ Προπύλαια νέα ἐστίν; πολλὰ ἱερά ἐστι. A neuter plural subject takes a singular verb.

**Exclamations with ὡς**: ὡς μέγα ἐστίν! 'how big it is!'.

exercises.prompt: Parse ἐξέρχεται.
exercises.explain: -εται: he or she goes out (ἐκ + ἔρχομαι).

exercises.prompt: ὁ Λύσις πρὸς ___ ἄγαλμα προσέρχεται.
exercises.explain: πρός takes the accusative: πρὸς τὸ ἄγαλμα.

exercises.prompt: ἀπὸ ___ ἀκροπόλεως καταβαίνουσιν.
exercises.explain: ἀπό takes the genitive: ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκροπόλεως.

exercises.explain: θύρᾳ is dative, so ἐπί means 'at, by': ἐπὶ τῇ θύρᾳ.

culture.title: The Acropolis in 432 BC
culture.md:
What Lysis and Elpis saw was almost new. The Persians had burnt the Acropolis in 480, and for a generation the Athenians left the ruins as they were. Then, from 447, Pericles' building programme covered the rock with marble. The **Parthenon** was structurally complete by 438, when Pheidias' gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos, twelve metres high, was set up inside it; the last of its pediment sculptures were being put in place in the very summer of our story. The **Propylaia**, the monumental gate-building by the architect Mnesikles, had been under construction since 437; work stopped when the war began in 431 and it was never finished — the unfinished lifting bosses are still on its walls today. Just inside the gate stood Pheidias' earlier **bronze Athena**, some nine metres tall, spear-tip glinting so that sailors rounding Sounion could see it.

One thing the new marble was not: the Parthenon was not the temple where the goddess was worshipped. Athena Polias, the guardian of the city, lived in her ancient olive-wood statue, kept in the old temple north of the Parthenon beside her sacred olive tree; the robe woven for the Panathenaia went to *that* image, and the building we call the Erechtheion would not be begun for another decade. The Parthenon, with its treasury and its colossal statue, was a votive gift on the grandest scale, a statement of what the city and its empire could afford. Ariston, who fired pots for a living, would have known exactly how much marble, gold and labour he was looking at.
